# RLHF and Reward Modeling {#sec-rlhf}

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) trains a language model on
preference data, the recorded comparisons between candidate responses. It adds
two learned systems: a reward model that estimates which responses the labeling
procedure would prefer, and a policy that is updated to receive higher estimated
reward. The policy is the language model being trained, described in
reinforcement-learning terms: given a prompt, it assigns a probability to every
possible response, and each response it generates is a sample from that
distribution. The reward model compresses comparisons into a scalar score.
Training then shifts the policy's probabilities toward responses that score
well.

The familiar recipe is to train a reward model on human comparisons, then
optimize the policy against that reward with
@gls-ppo, a reinforcement-learning algorithm described later in this chapter.
Some constitutional and @gls-rlaif variants have a model produce some of the
comparisons; the reward model's mathematical definition is unchanged. In the
classic recipe, a learned reward needs a KL constraint, a penalty on how far the
policy's output distribution moves from the model it started from, because the
score is a proxy learned on a limited response distribution. Neither the
constraint nor PPO makes that proxy correct.

This chapter keeps three objects separate: the preference record is a
measurement, the reward model is an estimator fitted to those measurements,
and the policy objective sets how aggressively the estimate is used.
@sec-behavior-specs covered the first object. This chapter starts with the
second and follows it through the online policy update, in which the policy is
trained on responses it samples as training proceeds (on-policy data).

## RLHF learns a judge, then trains a policy

For some open-ended tasks, comparing two candidate responses is more practical
than writing an ideal answer. A labeler can often identify the clearer summary
or the more useful explanation even when several answers would be acceptable.
That advantage is task-dependent. A vague rubric, missing expertise, or a
forced choice between equally good responses still produces a poor label.

The classic assistant-training pipeline has three stages:

1. **Supervised fine-tuning.** Demonstrations produce an assistant-shaped model,
   as described in @sec-sft-peft.
2. **Reward modeling.** Labelers compare responses sampled for the same prompt.
   A reward model learns to predict those comparisons.
3. **Policy optimization.** The current policy samples new responses. The
   frozen reward model scores them, a frozen reference (a fixed copy of the SFT
   model) measures how far the policy has drifted, and a policy-gradient
   optimizer updates the policy so that high-scoring responses become more
   probable.

Only the third stage is reinforcement learning. The reward-model stage is
supervised learning on comparison labels. The stages also fail in different
ways: the labels may express the wrong criterion, the reward model may
generalize poorly, or the policy may exploit an error in an otherwise useful
reward model.

## Train a scorer from comparisons

Let a reward-model dataset contain $N$ comparisons:

$$
\mathcal{D}=\{(x_i,y_i^+,y_i^-)\}_{i=1}^N,
$$

where $x_i$ is prompt $i$; $y_i^+$ is the response preferred under the
annotation procedure; $y_i^-$ is the other response; and $N$ is the number of
recorded comparisons. A reward model $r_\phi(x,y)$ with parameters $\phi$
assigns one scalar to a prompt-response pair. The Bradley-Terry model
[@bradley1952rank] converts the difference between two scores into the
probability that one item is preferred. Under that model, define

$$
\Delta_i
=r_\phi(x_i,y_i^+)-r_\phi(x_i,y_i^-),
\qquad
p_i=\sigma(\Delta_i)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\Delta_i}},
$$

and minimize the average negative log-likelihood

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}(\phi)
=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i.
$$

Here $\Delta_i$ is the score difference; $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid; and
$p_i$ is the model's probability that the annotation procedure prefers
$y_i^+$ to $y_i^-$. The model is never told that either response deserves an
absolute reward such as 7. It is asked to make the observed winner more
probable than the loser.

A hard label, which records only the winner, discards uncertainty. If the same
pair receives $m_i$ valid votes and $n_i^+$ of them prefer $y_i^+$, a soft
target $q_i=n_i^+/m_i$ can retain the vote split:

$$
\mathcal{L}_i
=-q_i\log p_i-(1-q_i)\log(1-p_i).
$$

In this expression, $m_i$ is the vote count, $n_i^+$ is the number of votes for
$y_i^+$, and $q_i\in[0,1]$ is their fraction. A value of $q_i=0.5$ can represent
an even split or an explicit tie. It does not explain *why* annotators
disagreed, so the raw votes, annotator metadata, and reasons described in
@sec-behavior-specs should remain available.

Rankings require another qualification. InstructGPT showed a labeler between
four and nine responses, then derived every ordered pair implied by the ranking
[@ouyang2022training]. A ranking of $K$ candidates yields
$K(K-1)/2$ pairwise constraints, but not that many independent observations:
the pairs share the same prompt, candidates, and labeler. Ouyang et al. grouped
all pairs from one ranking into one training batch because treating them as
independent updates caused rapid overfitting. Rankings reduce the annotation
effort per pair, and the pairs from one ranking still count as one correlated
group of observations.

A reward-model validation report should include held-out log loss, pairwise
accuracy, and a calibration curve. Held-out log loss is the loss above computed
on comparisons excluded from training; a calibration curve compares predicted
preference probabilities with observed win rates. Accuracy alone treats a
probability of $0.51$ like $0.99$ when both select the same winner. Break the
report down by prompt source, task, response length, candidate policy, safety
category, and annotator group. RewardBench illustrates the need for structured
slices by testing reward models on chat, reasoning, and safety comparisons whose
winners sometimes differ for small but verifiable reasons
[@lambert2024rewardbench].

## Pairwise training determines only score differences

The loss depends on a score difference. For any prompt-only offset $c(x)$,

$$
r'_\phi(x,y)=r_\phi(x,y)+c(x)
$$

produces exactly the same comparison probabilities because $c(x)$ cancels.
Raw reward values therefore have no natural zero and should not be compared
across prompts. Under a correctly specified and calibrated logistic model, a
*difference* does have an interpretation: $\Delta=\log[p/(1-p)]$ is the fitted
log-odds. For example, $p=0.75$ corresponds to
$\Delta=\log 3\approx1.10$. This does not make either individual score an
absolute measure of response quality.

@fig-rlhf-reward-modeling-2 shows this invariance. Shifting both scores leaves
the fitted probability unchanged.

![The Bradley-Terry probability depends on the difference between two reward-model scores. Adding the same offset to both scores changes neither the difference nor the modeled preference probability. The individual scores are therefore not an absolute quality scale.](/figures/rlhf-reward-modeling-2.svg){#fig-rlhf-reward-modeling-2}

Implementations often choose a convenient zero after training. InstructGPT
shifted the reward-model bias so labeler demonstrations had mean reward zero
[@ouyang2022training]. Centering in this way changes no score difference and no
pairwise probability. Rescaling is different. Multiplying every reward by a
positive constant preserves the ranking but changes the fitted probabilities
and the reward's strength relative to the KL penalty, whose coefficient $\beta$
appears in the policy objective below. For reproducibility, reward scale and
$\beta$ must be recorded together.

The scalar itself is also an assumption. Bradley-Terry represents the compared
responses with one latent ordering. Cyclic preferences, context-dependent
criteria, and stable differences among annotators may not fit that ordering.
Pooling them can still yield a useful predictor, whose single score is an
average over those plural judgments.

## The policy objective has two terms

Once the reward model is frozen, the policy generates responses and receives
their learned scores. A common objective, averaged over prompts and the
responses the policy samples for them, is

$$
J(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_x,\,y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
\left[
r_\phi(x,y)
-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}
\right].
$$

Here $\mathcal{D}_x$ is the prompt distribution; $\pi_\theta$ is the policy
being optimized, with parameters $\theta$; $y$ is a response sampled from that
policy; $r_\phi$ is the frozen learned reward; $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is a frozen
reference policy, usually derived from SFT; and $\beta>0$ controls the strength
of the reference penalty. The first term rewards responses favored by the
learned judge. The second makes responses costly when the policy assigns them
much more probability than the reference does.

The distribution-level quantity is @gls-kl: how different the new token
distribution is from the reference distribution. Taking the expectation of the
sampled sequence log-ratio under $\pi_\theta$ gives
$\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})$. For an autoregressive response
$y=(y_1,\ldots,y_T)$,

$$
\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)}
=\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})}
{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})}.
$$

In this sum, $T$ is the response length; $y_t$ is token $t$; and $y_{<t}$ is
the preceding response prefix. Implementations use these sampled token
log-ratios as reward-shaping terms, per-token adjustments to the reward the
policy receives. A sampled log-ratio is not itself the KL divergence, and an
individual contribution can be negative. The KL is an expectation over tokens
sampled from the policy.

The penalty is a regularizer: it discourages large moves away from the
reference. A small measured KL does not show that the reward is correct, and a
large $\beta$ can prevent useful changes.
Some systems keep $\beta$ fixed; others adjust it to track a target KL. Either
way, the achieved KL, not only the configured coefficient, belongs in the run
record.

## KL and PPO clipping constrain different moves

PPO is one optimizer for the objective above [@schulman2017proximal]. It
introduces a third policy notation that is easy to confuse with the reference.
Here the rollout policy $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$ is a snapshot of the policy that
sampled the current batch of responses, the rollout batch. The reference
$\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the SFT anchor used across many batches. They usually
are not the same model.

PPO describes generation in reinforcement-learning terms: each token is an
action, taken in a state formed by the prompt and the tokens generated so far.
Here $a_t=y_t$ is the sampled token and $s_t=(x,y_{<t})$ is its
prompt-and-prefix state. Because PPO takes several gradient steps on one
rollout batch, it divides the probability the updated policy gives each sampled
token by the probability the snapshot gave it. That quotient is the importance
ratio

$$
\rho_t(\theta)
=\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a_t\mid s_t)}
$$

PPO then maximizes the clipped surrogate, a substitute objective computed from
the stored batch:

$$
L_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)
=\mathbb{E}_t\left[
\min\left(
\rho_t(\theta)\widehat{A}_t,
\operatorname{clip}(\rho_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)
\widehat{A}_t
\right)
\right].
$$

Here $\rho_t$ compares the updated policy with the rollout snapshot;
$\widehat{A}_t$ is an estimated advantage; $\epsilon>0$ is the clipping width;
and $\operatorname{clip}(z,l,u)$ truncates $z$ to the interval $[l,u]$. The
advantage estimates how much better a sampled token turned out than expected. It
compares the shaped return, the reward (including the KL shaping terms) that the
response collects from that token onward, with a baseline predicted by a critic,
a learned predictor of the expected return from the prefix alone. The comparison
reduces gradient variance without identifying which token caused the outcome.

The two controls solve different problems:

- The reference KL discourages cumulative semantic drift from the SFT policy.
- PPO clipping limits the incentive to change sampled likelihood ratios far
  beyond the clipping interval while reusing one rollout batch.

Clipping does not impose a hard trust region, meaning a guaranteed bound on how
far one update can move the policy, and does not guarantee that the final
policy stays within a chosen distance [@wang2019truly]. Learning rate, advantage
normalization, value estimation, batching, and numerical stability still
matter.

```{figure}
//| figure: ppo-clip
//| label: fig-rlhf-ppo-clip
//| fig-cap: "PPO's clipped surrogate for one sampled token, drawn from the equation above with the advantage set to +1 and to −1. The bold line is $L=\min(\rho\widehat{A},\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\widehat{A})$. In the hatched range it is flat, so the token gives no gradient that moves $\rho$ further, and which side is flat depends on the sign of $\widehat{A}$. The window is measured from the rollout snapshot $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$ and re-centers every batch, so in the lower panel the incentive limit on a token's log-ratio to the reference grows by $\ln(1\pm\epsilon)$ per batch and has no ceiling; the reference KL term is what measures that accumulated distance."
```

## Four roles participate in the loop

Classic PPO-based RLHF has four parameter roles. Each role is a logical function
in the loop, and the last column lists the ways implementations realize it.

| Role | Updated during PPO? | Job | Implementation choices |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Policy $\pi_\theta$ | Yes | Generates responses and receives policy-gradient updates | Full model, adapters, or sharded actor |
| Reference $\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ | No | Supplies log-probabilities for the drift penalty | Frozen copy, shared frozen weights, sharded or offloaded model |
| Reward model $r_\phi$ | No | Scores complete prompt-response pairs | Separate scalar model, smaller model, or ensemble |
| Critic $V_\psi$ | Yes | Predicts shaped return from prefixes | Separate value model or value head sharing a backbone |

The rollout snapshot $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$ is another logical policy state, but
stored rollout log-probabilities can represent it during optimization. InstructGPT
used a 6B reward model and a 6B value model even when training a 175B policy
[@ouyang2022training]. That design shows that “four roles” does not mean
“four copies of the policy.” Sharing, sharding, adapters, offloading, and
recomputation change peak memory and throughput.

@fig-rlhf-pipeline shows the data flow. Dashed boxes stay frozen during a PPO
update; the policy and critic receive gradients.

```{dot}

  reward [label="reward r_φ\nfrozen", style="rounded,filled,dashed"];
  reference [label="reference π_ref\nfrozen", style="rounded,filled,dashed"];

  { rank=same; prefs; sft; }
  { rank=same; rmtrain; policy; }
  { rank=same; reward; critic; reference; }

  prefs -> rmtrain -> reward;
  sft -> policy;
  sft -> reference [style=dashed];
  policy -> sample;
  sample -> reward [label="score"];
  sample -> critic [label="prefixes"];

  update -> critic [constraint=false];
}
```

## From trajectory preferences to instruction following

Reward learning from comparisons predates its use in chat models. Christiano et
al. trained reward predictors from human comparisons of short trajectory
segments, then optimized agents in Atari and simulated locomotion tasks against
the learned rewards [@christiano2017deep]. Ziegler et al. brought the method to
language tasks including stylistic continuation and summarization
[@ziegler2019finetuning]. Stiennon et al. then built the recognizable language
pipeline for summarization: collect pairwise judgments, train a reward model,
and optimize a language policy with PPO and a reference penalty
[@stiennon2020summarize].

InstructGPT broadened that recipe from a specific task to a distribution of API
instructions and made the SFT, reward-model, and PPO sequence widely known. Its
1.3B PPO-ptx model was preferred to the 175B GPT-3 baseline by labelers on its
held-out API prompt distribution [@ouyang2022training]. That result demonstrates
the value of post-training on the measured distribution. It does not show that
the smaller model had greater general capability. The same paper reported
regressions on some public NLP tasks and simple mistakes outside the main
preference comparison.

Constitutional AI changed the source of part of the feedback. In its harmlessness
experiment, a model applied written principles to compare responses; those AI
comparisons trained a preference model that supplied the RL reward
[@bai2022constitutional]. This removed human harmlessness labels from that
stage, not human normative choices or evaluation. People still chose the
principles, and the setup retained human feedback for helpfulness. RLAIF names
that substitution of AI-produced feedback for some human-produced feedback.

PPO is one of several optimizers used with human feedback. RLOO and GRPO are
critic-free policy-gradient alternatives, but they construct baselines
differently: RLOO uses the mean return of the *other* samples, while GRPO
standardizes rewards within a same-prompt group [@ahmadian2024back;
@shao2024deepseekmath]. DAPO modifies the group-relative family for verifiable
reasoning and can remove the explicit reference term in that setting
[@yu2025dapo]. These methods are prominent in disclosed reasoning work; that
prominence does not establish that any one optimizer is used in every
post-training stack. @sec-training-to-reason covers them in their main
application. The offline alternative, which removes the explicit reward model
and online RL loop, begins in @sec-dpo-variants.

## Optimization tests the proxy outside its training distribution

A reward model is evaluated on held-out comparisons sampled from some candidate
distribution. Policy optimization changes that distribution. The reward model
then scores responses that were selected because they receive unusually high
predicted reward, which is a harder test than ordinary validation.

The failure has been observed directly in human evaluation. In summarization
experiments, Stiennon et al. trained policies at several optimization strengths.
Under light optimization, both learned reward and labeler preference improved.
With stronger optimization, predicted reward continued to improve while labeler
preference fell, eventually becoming anti-correlated with the proxy in that
experiment [@stiennon2020summarize].

Gao et al. studied the curve more systematically with a controlled substitute
for expensive repeated human evaluation. A fixed gold reward model stood in for
human judgment and generated labels used to train a separate proxy reward
model. Optimizing the proxy eventually reduced the independent gold-model score,
for both RL and best-of-$n$ selection (sampling $n$ responses and keeping the
one the proxy scores highest), and the curve changed with model size, data
size, optimizer, and KL penalty [@gao2022scaling]. This demonstrates proxy
over-optimization in a synthetic gold-model setup. It does not measure a
universal curve of true human quality.

```{figure}
//| figure: reward-overoptimization
//| label: fig-rlhf-overoptimization
//| fig-cap: "Proxy and gold reward-model scores as a policy is optimized away from its initial policy, in Gao et al.'s synthetic setup, where a fixed 6B gold reward model stands in for human labelers and a 1.2B policy is optimized against a smaller proxy [@gao2022scaling]. The dashed and solid curves are one measured run, traced from the paper's figures. The dotted curve is the paper's fitted law for the gold score with its coefficients for each reward-model size: $R(d)=d(a-b\ln d)$ for RL and $R(d)=d(a-bd)$ for best-of-$n$, where $d$ is the square root of the KL and $a$, $b$ are the paper's $\alpha$, $\beta$; the RL $a$, one constant across sizes, is recovered from the paper's curves. The lower panel is the run's KL against PPO steps or against $n$. A KL coefficient $\beta>0$, run only with the 1.2B reward model, halts the policy at a fixed distance on the same gold curve. Gold scores are a model's judgment, not human quality."
```

The small program below plots both curves. Its quadratic gold curve is a
schematic and does not reproduce Gao et al.'s fitted coefficients. Changing
`curvature` moves the peak of the gold curve, which shows why there is no
universal stopping point.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

policy_shift = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
proxy_score = 0.35 + 0.12 * policy_shift
curvature = 0.016  # illustrative, not an estimate from Gao et al.
gold_score = 0.45 + 0.16 * policy_shift - curvature * policy_shift**2
best = int(np.argmax(gold_score))

plt.plot(policy_shift, proxy_score, label="optimized proxy score")
plt.plot(policy_shift, gold_score, label="independent gold-model score")
plt.axvline(policy_shift[best], ls="--", color="gray")
plt.xlabel("policy shift from reference")
plt.ylabel("score (illustrative units)")
plt.title("A proxy can improve after its independent check worsens")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

print(f"gold-model score peaks near shift={policy_shift[best]:.1f}")
```
::::

Reward hacking is the behavioral consequence of this generalization gap. The
policy may discover verbosity, confident phrasing, formatting, agreement with a
user, or another feature that raises reward without improving the intended
task. Sycophancy is one measured example: human and learned preference judgments
sometimes favored a convincing answer that agreed with the user over a correct
one, and optimization against the preference model could amplify that trade-off
[@sharma2024sycophancy]. This is evidence about one path to sycophancy, not a
claim that RLHF is its only cause. Reward *tampering*, in which an agent changes
the scoring process itself, is a separate problem from exploiting a fixed
misspecified score.

## What the controls can and cannot do

Each control addresses a different failure. None replaces an evaluation that
is independent of the optimized reward.

| Control | What it can address | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Better rubrics, expert labels, ties, and reasons | Measurement errors and missing distinctions | Generalization to responses the collection never covered |
| Held-out RM log loss, accuracy, and calibration by slice | Predictive failure before RL begins | Robustness to policy-selected high-score outputs |
| Fresh on-policy comparisons and reward-model refreshes | Coverage of behaviors produced by the changing policy | Correctness of the external judge or rubric |
| Reference KL and a tuned $\beta$ | Drift away from a known policy distribution | Validity of the reward or retention of every base capability |
| PPO clipping and conservative learning rates | Instability while reusing rollout batches | A hard trust region or protection from reward hacking |
| Early stopping on independent evaluations | Observed divergence between proxy and external quality | Failures outside the evaluation slices |
| Diverse reward-model ensembles | Some model-specific errors and uncertainty | Shared blind spots or contested value choices |
| Pre-training-data mixing | Regressions on capabilities represented by that data | Better preference alignment by itself |

A reward-model ensemble combines the scores of several reward models, and it
controls only part of the problem. Coste et al. found that conservative
objectives over reward-model ensembles reduced over-optimization in a synthetic
gold-reward setup, with particularly strong results for best-of-$n$ selection
[@coste2023ensembles]. Shared training data and shared
rubrics can still produce shared errors.

The “alignment tax” is likewise an empirical regression, not a universal law
that safety must reduce capability. InstructGPT used the term for lower scores
on specific public NLP datasets. Mixing pre-training gradients into PPO greatly
reduced those regressions without reducing labeler preference, although some
gaps remained. Increasing the KL coefficient alone did not recover the same
tasks and reduced validation reward [@ouyang2022training]. Over-refusal is a
different failure: a miscalibrated safety boundary under which the model
declines requests it should answer.

Which post-training method produces that regression is itself measurable.
Shenfeld et al. fine-tuned the same base models on the same new tasks with
supervised fine-tuning and with on-policy RL, which trains on responses sampled
from the current policy. They matched the new-task score, then measured what had
been lost on prior tasks. The RL runs retained more. In their explanation,
forgetting tracked the KL divergence between the fine-tuned and the base policy,
measured on the new task, rather than the number of steps, the learning rate, or
the size of the weight change. Supervised fine-tuning has no term that keeps the
policy near the base, so the solution it converges to for the new task can lie
arbitrarily far from the base policy. On-policy RL reweights what the current
policy already produces, which biases it toward the KL-nearest solution that
satisfies the reward. The authors name the bias RL's Razor and report it for
language models and for robotic control [@shenfeld2025rlrazor].

This result gives the reference-KL row in the table above a second role. An
explicit $\beta$ penalizes drift on purpose, while on-policy sampling limits
drift as a side effect of where the gradients come from. The achieved KL that a
run reports therefore measures how far the optimizer moved the policy and also
predicts how much prior-task performance the model retains. The finding is a
correlation established over particular task pairs, so it suggests which recipe
to try first and does not replace evaluation on the prior tasks.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

The existence of reward over-optimization is well supported in particular
human-evaluated and synthetic gold-model experiments. What remains unsettled is
how far the controls above scale. One view treats reward modeling as an
iterative measurement problem: expand coverage with on-policy data, estimate
uncertainty, update the judge, and stop against independent evaluation. The
more skeptical view notes that the policy and the proxy keep co-evolving, while
human-defined quality remains expensive and incomplete to measure.

Goodhart's law is a useful warning that an optimized proxy can stop tracking its
target. It is not a theorem that every finite reward model must fail at one
fixed KL value. The location and shape of a divergence depend on the feedback,
reward model, policy, and optimizer. Direct preference objectives remove some
RLHF machinery, but they do not remove this measurement problem.
:::

## Use external judgment to decide when to stop

A practical run begins with a gate on the reward model and ends with a gate that
does not use that reward model. One defensible procedure is:

1. Split prompts by source and near-duplicate family before training the reward
   model.
2. Fit the reward model on grouped comparisons or rankings, preserving ties and
   raw votes.
3. Report held-out log loss, accuracy, calibration, and slice results. Do not
   begin RL if critical slices fail.
4. Freeze the chosen reward-model version, reference version, tokenizer, chat
   template, and reward normalization.
5. Sample responses from $\pi_{\mathrm{old}}$, then record the prompt, response,
   reward score, reference log-probabilities, rollout log-probabilities, and
   model versions.
6. Compute shaped returns and critic-based advantages, apply limited PPO
   updates, and measure the achieved policy-to-reference KL.
7. At fixed intervals, run held-out human or task evaluation plus capability and
   safety regression suites.
8. Add audited on-policy comparisons when the policy reaches response regions
   the reward model did not cover; version and retrain the reward model rather
   than silently changing it mid-run.
9. Stop or roll back when external quality flattens or declines, even if the
   learned reward continues to rise.

The run dashboard should keep proxy and external evidence in separate panels:

| Signal | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Reward-model training and validation loss | Whether the learned judge is fitting and generalizing on recorded comparisons |
| Pairwise accuracy and calibration by slice | Where fitted preference probabilities work or fail |
| Mean reward and reward distribution | What the optimizer is successfully increasing |
| Realized sequence and token-level KL | How far the policy has moved from the reference under the chosen estimator |
| Independent preference win rate or task metric | Whether behavior improved outside the optimized proxy |
| Capability and safety regressions | What changed outside the preference target |

The stopping rule belongs to the external rows. A rising reward curve proves
that optimization is working against its score. It does not prove that the
model is getting better.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

The systems layer shapes which RLHF formulation is practical. A classic PPO
loop needs forward passes through the policy, reference, reward model, and
critic, plus autoregressive rollout generation. Those are four logical roles,
but peak residency depends on sharding, sharing, adapters, offloading, and
whether log-probabilities are stored or recomputed. Generation and model
coordination can therefore cost more wall time and memory than the short loss
formula suggests.

This cost motivates two different simplifications. Direct preference methods in
@sec-dpo-variants remove the explicit reward model, critic, and online rollout
loop. Critic-free policy-gradient methods such as RLOO and GRPO retain online
sampling but replace the learned value baseline. Some formulations retain a
reference and some verifier-based descendants do not, so “three models instead
of four” is not a universal accounting rule. Measure the actual execution plan
against the training and serving systems in @sec-training-at-scale and
@sec-serving-problem.
:::
